title: Story Points Revisited
summary: Ron Jeffries regrets story points: they were renamed ideal days, are misused for date prediction and team comparison, invite pressure that erodes quality, and are better replaced by slicing stories small and releasing often.

assertions.quote: we really only used the points to decide how much work to take into an iteration anyway
I think comparing teams on quality of estimates or velocity is harmful.

verdicts.note: Velocity is team-relative by construction; Goodhart effects on normalised points are widely reported.

Relative (story-point style) estimation is found no more accurate than absolute time estimation and prone to underestimating large items, supporting weak date prediction; comparing teams by velocity is not examined.

assertions.quote: Because estimates are at least implicated in the application of undue pressure, I'd prefer to avoid them.
I think tracking how actuals compare with estimates is at best wasteful

verdicts.note: The opposite of Kaplan-Moss's calibration advice; no outcome data either way.

A company that paid bonuses for estimate accuracy saw accuracy improve while productivity fell because managers padded estimates and absorbed the buffer; accountability raised accuracy mainly by adjusting work content and quality to fit the estimate.

Review finds accuracy evaluation improves software estimation accuracy but partly via self-fulfilling prophecy, and that strong accountability pressure or reward/punishment should be avoided because evaluation pressure degrades difficult judgements.

assertions.quote: the team tries to go faster, and wind up skimping on code quality and on tests. They soon begin shipping more defects
slice stories down until they just need a single acceptance test

verdicts.note: Small batches improve flow in lean research; whether slicing fully replaces estimation is unproven.

Small software tasks were predicted without bias in the reviewed data while larger ones overran ~20%, which supports slicing for predictability; flow and removing the need for estimates are not examined.

assertions.quote: the important thing in Real Agile is to pick the next few things to do, and do them promptly
we do best to provide small amounts of value frequently, not wait for Big Bang releases that seem often to recede indefinitely into the future

verdicts.note: DORA and lean batch-size evidence favour small frequent releases.

In a two-project comparison the agile team that delivered in-progress software more often demonstrated business value sooner and saw a sharp rise in customer satisfaction, and a survey found agile companies prefer more releases; small, uncontrolled studies.

Deployment frequency is one of the four metrics whose high-performer cluster is twice as likely to meet organisational goals, which supports more frequent releases delivering more value; release size and receding dates are not measured as such.
